open-ds.why: radius.4: We use a 4px corner for Aster's buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a calm, precise tone, by brand convention. A small radius does this by softening the edge just enough while the sides stay straight. So Aster feels exact and steady, the least round of the three brands, because each brand sets its corners (shape.values) on a neutral base (brand.q1).

radius.4: We use the 4px control corner for Aster's badges in order to keep one role family by the badge relation: here badges share the control's corner. The same small radius does this by giving a plan status the box shape of the buttons. So a status reads as a small square tag, because each brand sets its three corners (shape.roles) and Aster's are small (shape.values).

radius.4: We use a 4px corner for Aster's menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 8px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by following the outer curve at the padding's distance. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because Aster's surfaces take 8px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.4: We use the 4px control corner for Aster's growing boxes in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving a list item or a text area the curve of the controls beside it. So fields and rows read as one family, because Aster's control corner is small, not a pill (shape.values).

radius.8: We use an 8px corner for Aster's cards and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a calm tone by brand convention. A modest radius does this by breaking the outline with a curve twice the 4px control corner. So a plan card reads as one object without feeling soft, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and each brand colors a neutral base (brand.q1).

open-ds.why: radius.12: We use a 12px corner for Birch's buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a friendly tone, by brand convention. A rounded radius does this by curving the edge clearly while the box keeps straight sides. So Birch feels softer than Aster yet still precise enough to fill a form, because each brand sets its corners (shape.values) on a neutral base (brand.q1).

radius.pill: We use a pill corner for Birch's badges in order to give status a role of its own, apart from the 12px controls. A full radius does this by rounding both ends into a capsule. So a status and a button never look alike, because each brand sets three corners (shape.roles) and Birch rounds its badges (shape.values).

radius.12: We use a 12px corner for Birch's menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 16px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by the nesting rule of Aster's option corner, run 4px inside Birch's 16px surface. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because Birch's surfaces take 16px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.12: We use the 12px control corner for Birch's growing boxes in order to keep their role, as objects of one family, by inheritance from the control corner. The same radius does this by giving Birch's list items and text areas the 12px curve of its controls. So fields and rows read as one family, because Birch's control corner is rounded, not a pill (shape.values).

radius.16: We use a 16px corner for Birch's cards and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a friendly tone by brand convention. A larger radius does this by breaking the outline with a curve wider than the 12px controls. So a plan card reads as one soft object, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) and each brand colors a neutral base (brand.q1).

coral.label: Coral
coral.description: Upbeat and energetic: coral orange, Poppins, pill controls.

theme.$description: The Coral theme: what each brand-dependent semantic key picks, in light and dark, plus mode-free picks (fonts, corners) in base. Info uses blue, kept apart from the brand color so it never reads as an action. Categories 1 to 5 are teal, purple, orange, blue, green: distinct hues for tags and chart series, with no meaning. Disabled uses the neutral slate.

open-ds.why: radius.pill: We use a pill corner for Coral's buttons and inputs in order to mark their role as controls in a playful tone, by brand convention. A full radius does this by rounding both ends of every Coral button and input into a capsule. So Coral feels upbeat, the roundest of the three brands, because each brand sets its corners (shape.values) on a neutral base (brand.q1).

radius.pill: We use the pill control corner for Coral's badges in order to keep one role family by the badge relation: here badges share the control's corner. The same full radius does this by giving a status the capsule of the buttons. So the shape matches the buttons and the word in each badge marks it as a status, because each brand sets its corners (shape.roles, shape.values).

radius.16: We use a 16px corner for Coral's menu options in order to keep nesting by the relation: the 20px surface corner minus the panel's 4px padding. The inner radius does this by the nesting rule of Aster's option corner, run 4px inside Coral's 20px surface. So an option's curve runs parallel to its menu's curve, because Coral's surfaces take 20px (shape.roles, brand.q1) and the panel's padding is 4px (spacing.values).

radius.12: We use the 12px box corner for Coral's growing boxes in order to keep them box-shaped objects by the relation: a pill control gives way to the box corner. A moderate radius does this by curving the corners while the sides stay straight as the box grows. So a text area stays a box, not an oval, because Coral's controls are pills (shape.values).

radius.20: We use a 20px corner for Coral's cards and dialogs in order to make each card read as a separate object, in a playful tone by brand convention. A large radius does this by breaking the outline with a wide curve while the sides stay straight. So a plan card reads as one round, friendly object, the roundest of the three brands, because containers get their own corner (shape.roles, shape.count) on a neutral base (brand.q1).

open-ds.why: Every brand shares small steps on a 4px grid, so the base is 4px. Comfortable density sets each multiple, with big steps for product pages.

We use 8px for the tight gap between the parts of one item in order to group and separate: two base steps (2 × 4px) on the shared grid. Distance does this by grouping what is near and separating what is far, as the eye reads proximity (Gestalt), so a gap between groups stays clearly larger than a gap inside one. So the shared parts look the same in every brand, because the brands share one set of steps on a 4px grid (spacing.definition) and three brands share one system (business.q2).

We use 12px for the default gap between the fields of one form group in order to group and separate: three base steps (3 × 4px), one step wider than the tight gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so customers on phones tap the right field, because the layout is comfortable (spacing.values) and customers sign up on phones (scenarios.q1).

We use 24px for the group gap between groups in a form in order to group and separate: six base steps (6 × 4px), twice the default gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so sign-up forms keep the same shape in every brand, because three brands share one system (business.q2) and the layout is comfortable (spacing.values).

We use 48px for the section gap between page sections in order to group and separate: twelve base steps (12 × 4px), twice the group gap. Distance does this by the rule given for space.gap.tight, so each offer card stands apart on a product page, because the layout is comfortable (spacing.values) and the 4px grid holds big steps for product pages (spacing.definition).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside controls in order to give content room inside its box: four base steps (4 × 4px), the same as a table cell. Padding does this by keeping content off the edge of its box, so the content reads as part of that box, and by setting the size of the box with the content. So buttons are the same size in every brand, because three brands share one system (business.q2) and steps sit on a 4px grid (spacing.definition).

We use 24px for the padding inside cards and dialogs in order to give content room inside its box: six base steps (6 × 4px), the same as the group gap. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so cards hold offers the same way in every brand, because three brands share one system (business.q2) and the layout is comfortable (spacing.values).

We use 16px for the inline padding inside table cells in order to give content room inside its box: four base steps (4 × 4px), the same as a control. Padding does this by the rule given for space.inset.control-x, so account tables keep room between columns on a phone, because customers sign up on phones (scenarios.q1) and the layout is comfortable (spacing.values).
A touch target sets the 44px default. Compact is one 8px step below it; large equals the default, as brand color marks the main action. Rows are a decision of their own and stay one control tall.

default.$description: Height of buttons and inputs, and the smallest target.

open-ds.why: We use 44px for buttons and inputs in order to make a hit target: the touch target size, step 0 of the control scale, a 44px hit area. Height does this by setting the hit area a finger or a pointer must hit; WCAG measures the hit area, not the drawn box (2.5.8: 24px at AA; 2.5.5: 44px at AAA), and padding or a label can make it larger than the box. So every control fits a thumb in every brand, because the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values) and customers sign up on phones (scenarios.q1).

We use 36px for compact controls, such as a show-password button inside a field, in order to make a hit target: one 8px step below the 44px default on the control scale; the 36px box relies on the padding of the field around it for a touch-size hit area. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so the button fits inside the field in every brand, because three brands share one system (business.q2) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

large.$description: Height of large controls. Not used in this system, so it equals the default.

open-ds.why: We use 44px for large controls in order to make a hit target: the default's step on the control scale and the default's 44px hit area, as the scheme has no hero action. Height does this by the rule given for size.control.default, so every brand's forms keep one height, and brand color marks the main action, because three brands share one system (business.q2) and the smallest target is touch size (accessibility.values).

We use 44px for one table row in order to keep the eye on its row: a row is one 44px default control tall, as rows stay one control tall. Row height does this by making each row a band the eye follows across, and a hit target when the row is clickable (WCAG 2.5.8: 24px). So rows stay easy to tap on a phone, and a control sits in a row with no gap, because account tables need a row height (spacing.roles) and the layout is comfortable (spacing.values).
16px matches the 16px body text an icon sits beside, so one icon size serves every brand and every label.

hit-area.$description: The least hit area of a control. A control drawn smaller keeps its size; its hit area grows past it, never into a neighbour.

open-ds.why: We use a 44px hit area for controls drawn smaller, such as a checkbox, a radio or a switch, in order to make a hit target a fingertip can find: the WCAG 2.5.5 size. The hit area does this by growing past the drawn box through a pseudo-element, and rows in a group stand at least 44px apart, so no two targets overlap. So customers tap the right control on a phone, because targets are sized for touch (accessibility.values) and the layout leaves room for it (spacing.values).

feedback.$description: Hover, press and toggle feedback. At most 150ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 150ms (moderate) for hover, press and toggle feedback in order to confirm each action inside the productive limit of 150ms. The duration does this by ending the change before the eye leaves the control. So customers see each action land and never wait for it, because motion is for feedback and guidance, which makes the family productive (motion.roles), and feedback feels moderate (motion.values).

panels.$description: Menus, popovers, dialogs and drawers opening. At most 300ms in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use 300ms (relaxed) for menus, popovers, dialogs and other panels in order to show where a panel comes from, inside the productive limit of 300ms. The duration does this by giving the eye just enough frames to follow the panel from its trigger. So customers move through sign-up the same way in every brand, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and there are two speeds (motion.count).

exit.$description: A layer closing. About 150ms, never more, in a productive family.

open-ds.why: We use the feedback duration, 150ms (moderate), for a layer that closes in order to finish the exit move within the productive 150ms. The duration does this by removing the layer in fewer frames than an open takes, as nothing in it needs reading any more. So customers get the page back at once, because productive exits stay short (motion.roles) and there are two speeds (motion.count).

standard.$description: The transition move: a state that changes in place, such as hover, press or toggle.

open-ds.why: We use the standard easing (0.2, 0, 0, 1) for state changes in place in order to do the transition move. The curve does this by reaching its target early and settling slowly, with no overshoot. So a hover, a press or a toggle lands at once and then stays still, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) and the family is productive (motion.roles).

enter.$description: The enter move: a layer that appears.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a panel that appears in order to do the enter move. The curve does this by spending most of the change in the first frames, so the layer is in place before it slows. So customers can read a menu almost as soon as it opens, because easing is a standard ease-out (motion.definition) in a productive family (motion.roles).

exit.$description: The exit move: a layer that closes in place.

open-ds.why: We use the strong-out easing (0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) for a layer that closes in place in order to do the exit move of the productive family. The curve does this by covering most of the way in the first third of its time, then easing to a stop. So a closed popover is gone before the next click, because productive exits take a strong ease-out (motion.roles) and easing never springs here (motion.definition).

exit-offscreen.$description: The exit move of a layer that slides off the screen: a sheet or a drawer.

open-ds.why: We use the exit move's strong-out easing for a drawer or sheet that slides off the screen, in order to keep every exit of a productive family on one fast curve. The curve does this by moving fastest at the start, so the panel clears the view with no slow tail. So the content under a closing sheet comes back at once, because only an expressive family accelerates what leaves the screen (motion.roles), and easing is a plain ease-out (motion.definition).

emphasize.$description: The emphasize move: a moment that calls for attention.

open-ds.why: We use the transition move's standard easing for a moment that calls for attention in order to give the emphasize move no overshoot. The curve does this by stopping at its target without passing it. So a new message draws the eye by its change, not by a bounce, because the family is productive (motion.roles) and easing is a standard ease-out, never a spring (motion.definition).
